text.p: Metal products and electronic equipment maker Hills Industries Ltd sees sensible and controlled growth through the next few years, with growing opportunities for its electronic arm and a new focus on exports.
"There is nothing I perceive will occur which means a strategy of sensible and controlled growth cannot occur (to the year 2000)," managing director David Simmons told Reuters.
Hills has seen a strong surge in its share price in recent months, rising from A$1.62 following the 5-for-1 split in its shares in November. The stock was trading at A$2.00 on Tuesday.
Simmons attributed part of the rise to the share split, but said he believed the stock had also been re-rated after its strong 1995/96 result, with a net profit of A$12.2 million.

Broker JB Were and Son last week issued a bullish report on Hills, upgrading its investment view to buy from hold, and lifting its forecast 1996/97 net profit to A$15 million from A$12 million, rising to A$16.5 million in 1997/98.
Hills posted a net profit of A$12.04 million in 1994/95.

Analyst Lou Capparelli said key factors in the upgrade were immediate results being generated by divestment of non-core assets, leverage to the improving housing and construction sector, organic growth and exciting overseas opportunities for Hills' electronics division and sound management.

Despite its exposure to the soft housing and retail sectors Hills showed further strength in its 1996/97 interim results, with a 13 percent rise in attributable profit to A$7.5 million. Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) for Hills' consumer products division were up 58 percent to A$3.3 million, industrial division down one percent to A$5.9 million and
electronics up 12 percent to A$4.9 million.

Simmons said the rise for consumer products, which include the traditional Hills' clothes hoist, had come off a very low base which "could not have got much worse" and, with sales down, growth had come through restructuring and cost-cutting.
Nonetheless he said the business still needed a dramatic improvement, and the company was aiming to lift the current EBIT to sales ratio of 5.5 percent to 10 percent in the medium term.
While Hills expects a modest upturn in housing from the last quarter of calendar 1997, he said it does not envisage a boom and the division was lifting new product development.
In electronics, Simmons said deregulation of the pay-TV market offered significant, albeit potentially volatile, opportunities in niche sectors for Hills.
While the strongest growth would come in the next few years, the development of private pay-TV networks and freeing up of telecommunications promised continuing momentum, he said.

Simmons said that while the industrial unit was budgeting for a flat year result, some growth was expected as the housing market picked up and the company had no plans to divest it as its large number of customers provided a degree of security.
Hills has made no secret of its interest in boosting growth through acquisition, although Simmons played down the prospect of a major acqusition to add a fourth business leg.
"For us, three segments have enough growth in them for us to be comfortable," he said.

In its latest corporate move, Hills has launched an unconditional bid for minority shares in metal products maker Woodroffe Industries Ltd, off a pre-bid stake of 49.82 percent. While full ownership was not a crucial issue, Simmons warned Hills would not necessarily continue to guarantee increased loan facilities for Woodroffe if the bid failed.
He said no-one should draw any conclusion from the Woodroffe bid about a future offer for Korvest Ltd, in which Hills has a 47.2 percent stake.

Simmons said Hills was aiming to lift its offshore revenue, both in exports to Asia (through electronics) and South America (consumer products) and pursuing the European clothesline market through its Wales-based manufacturing base.
While the Wales operation was not a star operator, he said there was no plan to divest because of its strategic position.
"If our strategy is to internationalise our business, why cut something off that has the real chance to do that?" he said.
